[THOUGHT]  
This is a 6-month non-healing lower-leg ulcer in a patient with objective evidence of **chronic venous insufficiency (CVI)** — confirmed by Doppler ultrasound showing *both reflux and obstruction* in superficial and deep venous systems, unilateral (right-dominant) edema, and diminished (but palpable) distal pulses. The wound lacks signs of active infection (no pain, erythema, warmth, drainage; negative culture), systemic illness, or dermatologic comorbidities. Critically, the **biopsy histopathology is pending**, and no clinical or imaging features suggest alternative primary etiologies (e.g., arterial ischemia — pulses present; neuropathy — no diabetes reported or confirmed; vasculitis — no systemic symptoms or extralesional findings; malignancy — highly suspicious *but unconfirmed*). While Marjolin ulcer (SCC arising in chronic venous ulcer) is a key concern given duration, it remains *speculative without histology*. The most parsimonious, evidence-supported diagnosis — grounded *only in what is confirmed* — is **chronic venous stasis ulcer**, as all objective vascular data align perfectly with CVI, and no contradictory findings exist. All other considerations (malignancy, occult infection, metabolic disease) are important *differential possibilities*, but none are supported by current evidence — they are either unconfirmed (HbA1c, biopsy), absent (fever, lymphadenopathy, satellite lesions), or ruled out by available data (negative culture, no arterial insufficiency signs). - Doppler ultrasound confirms venous reflux *and* obstruction in both superficial and deep systems of the right leg — diagnostic of chronic venous insufficiency/post-thrombotic syndrome.  
- Unilateral (right-worse) lower extremity edema — hallmark of CVI.  
- Diminished but palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses — argues against critical arterial insufficiency as primary cause.  
- No systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats) — reduces likelihood of occult infection or malignancy *at this stage*.  
- Negative wound culture (aerobic/anaerobic/fungal) — makes acute or routine bacterial/fungal infection unlikely as driver of non-healing.  
- No reported history of diabetes, autoimmune disease, or prior skin cancer — no supporting evidence for alternate major etiologies.  

[GAPS]  
- Histopathology report from skin biopsy — essential to rule out squamous cell carcinoma (e.g., Marjolin ulcer), vasculitis, or granulomatous disease.  
- Ankle-brachial index (ABI) — needed to definitively exclude concomitant arterial disease, despite palpable pulses.  
- HbA1c and fasting glucose — required to confirm or refute occult diabetes, a major modifier of wound healing.  
- Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) — would help assess subclinical inflammation or occult infection.  
- Special stains or PCR on biopsy tissue (e.g., AFB, PAS, GMS) — not yet performed or reported, limiting evaluation for mycobacterial or fungal etiologies.  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Chronic venous stasis ulcer

This is a 6-month non-healing lower-leg ulcer in a patient with objective evidence of **chronic venous insufficiency (CVI)** — confirmed by Doppler ultrasound showing *both reflux and obstruction* in superficial and deep venous systems, unilateral (right-dominant) edema, and diminished (but palpable) distal pulses. Critically, the **biopsy histopathology is pending**, and no clinical or imaging features suggest alternative primary etiologies (e.g., arterial ischemia — pulses present; neuropathy — no diabetes reported or confirmed; vasculitis — no systemic symptoms or extralesional findings; malignancy — highly suspicious *but unconfirmed*). While Marjolin ulcer (SCC arising in chronic venous ulcer) is a key concern given duration, it remains *speculative without histology*. The most parsimonious, evidence-supported diagnosis — grounded *only in what is confirmed* — is **chronic venous stasis ulcer**, as all objective vascular data align perfectly with CVI, and no contradictory findings exist. All other considerations (malignancy, occult infection, metabolic disease) are important *differential possibilities*, but none are supported by current evidence — they are either unconfirmed (HbA1c, biopsy), absent (fever, lymphadenopathy, satellite lesions), or ruled out by available data (negative culture, no arterial insufficiency signs). Thus, the provisional diagnosis must reflect the single most likely *established* etiology — not the most dangerous or highest-risk possibility.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Chronic (>6 months), non-healing wound on right lower leg — classic location for venous stasis ulcers.  
- Doppler ultrasound confirms venous reflux *and* obstruction in both superficial and deep systems of the right leg — diagnostic of chronic venous insufficiency/post-thrombotic syndrome.  
- Unilateral (right-worse) lower extremity edema — hallmark of CVI.  
- Diminished but palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses — argues against critical arterial insufficiency as primary cause.  
- No systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats) — reduces likelihood of occult infection or malignancy *at this stage*.  
- Negative wound culture (aerobic/anaerobic/fungal) — makes acute or routine bacterial/fungal infection unlikely as driver of non-healing.  
- No reported history of diabetes, autoimmune disease, or prior skin cancer — no supporting evidence for alternate major etiologies.  

[GAPS]  
- Histopathology report from skin biopsy — essential to rule out squamous cell carcinoma (e.g., Marjolin ulcer), vasculitis, or granulomatous disease.  
- Ankle-brachial index (ABI) — needed to definitively exclude concomitant arterial disease, despite palpable pulses.  
- HbA1c and fasting glucose — required to confirm or refute occult diabetes, a major modifier of wound healing.  
- Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) — would help assess subclinical inflammation or occult infection.  
- Special stains or PCR on biopsy tissue (e.g., AFB, PAS, GMS) — not yet performed or reported, limiting evaluation for mycobacterial or fungal etiologies.  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Chronic venous stasis ulcer
